title: Leek and bacon tart
subtitle: savoury leek and lardons in a shortcrust pastry case
excerpt: Leek and bacon tart is a blind-baked shortcrust case filled with softened leeks, lardons, and a cream and egg custard baked until just set. You get a slice that holds its shape cleanly and tastes of the filling rather than the pastry. Watch the custard temperature: too high and it will curdle and weep liquid rather than setting smooth.
sourceNotes: Savoury tarts in the French style, with a cream and egg custard filling baked in a blind-baked pastry case, appear across French regional cookery. The leek and lardon combination is a standard variation of this format, related to the quiche Lorraine tradition. The method follows the standard approach documented in French and British home-baking references.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Blind bake the pastry case the day before and keep it at room temperature, covered. Prepare the leek and lardon filling up to 24 hours ahead and refrigerate. Assemble and bake the custard on the day.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: Conventional oven, 190 degrees Celsius for blind baking. Reduce to 160 degrees Celsius conventional (145 degrees Celsius fan) to bake the custard filling. The lower temperature is essential for a smooth, uncurdled set.

glossaryTerms.definition: Baking an unfilled pastry case so the crust sets before any wet filling goes in. The case is lined with baking paper and weighted with ceramic beans or dried pulses so the base stays flat and the sides do not slump.

A pastry made by rubbing cold fat into flour until the mixture resembles breadcrumbs, then binding with the minimum amount of cold water. The fat limits gluten development, giving a crumbly, tender result.

A mixture of eggs, cream, and milk that sets when baked. The proteins in the eggs coagulate as they heat, turning the liquid into a firm but tender set. Baking at a low temperature prevents the proteins from tightening too quickly, which would cause the custard to curdle and produce a grainy or watery result.

go in. The leeks must be cooked until completely soft before the custard goes in: raw or underdone leeks release water into the custard during baking and can make the base soggy. The lardons add salt and richness, so hold back on additional seasoning until you have tasted the filling mix.
Making the pastry and blind baking

Rub the cold cubed butter into the flour and salt with your fingertips until the mixture looks like rough breadcrumbs. Add the beaten egg and cold water a tablespoon at a time, cutting through with a knife, until the dough just comes together. Press into a disc, wrap, and refrigerate for 30 minutes.

Preheat the oven to 190 degrees Celsius conventional. Roll the chilled pastry to a circle about 3 mm thick. Line a 23 cm loose-bottomed tart tin, trim the overhang, and prick the base. Line with crumpled baking paper and fill with baking beans. Set on a baking tray and blind bake for 15 minutes.
Remove the paper and beans and bake for a further 5 minutes until the base is dry and just turning pale gold. Remove from the oven. Reduce the oven temperature to 160 degrees Celsius.

Melt the 30 g of butter in a medium saucepan over medium-low heat. Add the sliced leeks with a pinch of salt. Cover and cook gently for 10 to 12 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the leeks are completely soft and have given up most of their liquid. Remove the lid and cook for a further 2 minutes to drive off remaining moisture.

In a separate pan or push the leeks to one side, fry the lardons over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes until they are cooked through and starting to colour. Drain off any excess fat. Combine the lardons with the leeks and leave to cool slightly.
Making the custard and baking the tart

Whisk together the 3 eggs, double cream, whole milk, a grating of nutmeg, and a small pinch each of salt and pepper. Taste the custard mixture; it should be lightly seasoned as the lardons will add more salt during baking.

Spread the leek and lardon mixture evenly over the base of the warm blind-baked case. Set the tart tin on the oven shelf pulled out slightly, then pour the custard over the filling until it reaches just below the rim. Slide the shelf in carefully.

Bake at 160 degrees Celsius for 28 to 32 minutes until the custard is set at the edges and barely trembles at the centre when the tin is gently moved. The surface should be lightly coloured rather than deep brown, and a knife inserted 3 cm from the edge should come out clean. Rest in the tin for 10 minutes before releasing and slicing.

attrs.heading: If something went wrong
attrs.intro: Four common problems with a savoury custard tart.

items.symptom: Custard is grainy and weeping liquid
items.cause: Baked at too high a temperature; the egg proteins over-tightened and expelled liquid.
items.fix: The custard baking temperature must be 160 degrees Celsius or below. An oven thermometer helps verify this.
items.avoid: Avoid baking custard fillings at the same temperature as the blind bake.

items.cause: Leeks not fully cooked before filling, or the blind bake was too short.
items.fix: Cook the leeks until all visible liquid has evaporated before using. The pastry base must be dry and set before the filling goes in.
items.avoid: Avoid rushing the leek cooking stage; cover off the moisture before adding the custard.

items.symptom: Custard overflows the case during baking
items.cause: Too much custard for the available space after the filling went in.
items.fix: Fill to just below the pastry rim, not flush with it. Pour in stages and leave 3 to 4 mm of space at the top.
items.avoid: Avoid filling from a large jug that is hard to control; use a smaller jug or ladle.

items.symptom: Tart does not release cleanly from the tin
items.cause: Not rested long enough, or filling still too soft.
items.fix: The 10-minute rest in the tin is important: the custard firms as it cools and the pastry contracts slightly from the sides.
items.avoid: Avoid trying to unmould immediately from the oven.
